PART 1 (number theory / algebra). Heading: 'The most elegant form of the solution of the general equation pp+qq+rr=0 is, with a and b arbitrary complex numbers:'
  p = (a-b)(b-a·i·i),  q = (b-b·i)(a·i·i-a·i),  r = (b·i-a)(a·i-b).
Here i = sqrt(-1), and 'aii' means a·i·i = -a. This reading is confirmed by the faint pencil marginalia aa-bb, 2ab, aa+bb written beside the three lines.

Expanding (my steps):
- p = (a-b)(b+a) = a^2-b^2.
- q = b(1-i)·a(i^2-i) = ab(1-i)(-1-i) = -ab(1-i)(1+i) = -2ab.
- r = (bi-a)(ai-b) = -ab - b^2 i - a^2 i + ab = -i(a^2+b^2).
Hence p^2+q^2+r^2 = (a^2-b^2)^2 + 4a^2b^2 - (a^2+b^2)^2 = 0.

So this is the classical parametrization of Pythagorean triples, (a^2-b^2)^2 + (2ab)^2 = (a^2+b^2)^2. It is rewritten for the complex 'sum of three squares = 0' form by multiplying the hypotenuse by i. Each of p, q, r is then written as a product of two linear factors of the shape (x·i^m - y·i^n). That quasi-cyclic pattern of powers of i is what makes it 'zierlichste'.

Generality (my remark): (p:q:r) runs over the whole conic x^2+y^2+z^2=0 in P^2(C). Scaling (a,b) by t scales (p,q,r) by t^2, and t^2 takes every complex value. So every complex solution arises, which justifies 'allgemeine'.

PART 2 (Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung). Let mu be the probability of an outcome E in one trial, so 1-mu is the probability that E fails. The probability that exactly k of n independent trials give E is
  phi(k) = n(n-1)...(n-k+1)/(1·2·...·k) · (1-mu)^(n-k) · mu^k = C(n,k) mu^k (1-mu)^(n-k).
Gauss then lists mean values (expectations):
- E[k] = n mu
- E[k(k-1)] = n(n-1) mu^2
- E[k(k-1)(k-2)] = n(n-1)(n-2) mu^3, and so on. In general the falling factorial moment is E[k^(m)] = n^(m) mu^m.
- E[(k-n mu)^2] = n mu(1-mu).

Implicit derivation (mine): differentiate the generating function (1-mu+mu x)^n m times at x=1. This gives n(n-1)...(n-m+1) mu^m. Then Var = E[k(k-1)] + E[k] - (E k)^2 = n(n-1)mu^2 + n mu - n^2 mu^2 = n mu(1-mu).

The section breaks off after these moment statements. The page has no stated purpose beyond these notes; the previous and next pages concern galvanometer circuits and circle geometry and are unrelated.
errors: The sign of q is -2ab, i.e. the parametrization yields q = -2ab rather than +2ab. This is irrelevant since only q^2 enters.
In the last line Gauss first wrote n mu(mu-...) and corrected it to n mu(1-mu); the corrected value is right.
'Allgemeine' (general) is justified over C. Over Gaussian integers this parametrization need not produce every primitive solution, but no such claim is made.

results.what: Complex parametrization of p^2+q^2+r^2=0 as p=(a-b)(b-a i^2), q=(b-bi)(a i^2-a i), r=(bi-a)(ai-b), i.e. (a^2-b^2, -2ab, -i(a^2+b^2))
results.modern_name: Rational parametrization of the conic x^2+y^2+z^2=0 / Pythagorean triple formula (Euclid's formula) in complex form
results.usually_credited_to: Euclid (Elements X, Lemma 1 to Prop. 29) / Diophantus; the general conic parametrization is classical

results.modern_name: Factorial moments of the binomial distribution
results.usually_credited_to: Classical (de Moivre / Laplace era); the explicit factorial-moment formalism is later (19th–20th c.)

deep.surprise_reason: Both items are standard. The first is the Pythagorean-triple parametrization recast elegantly with powers of i. The second is the binomial distribution with its factorial moments and variance, well known since de Moivre and Laplace. The only mildly notable feature is Gauss's aesthetic factorized form with i-powers and his systematic listing of factorial moments, a natural Gaussian touch but not a new result.
